client: I've been feeling really lost ever since my grandmother passed away last month. It's like this heavy sadness that just won't lift, and I keep finding myself questioning what the point of everything is, what my future even looks like without her in it. I'm not sure talking about it is really going to change anything, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds incredibly heavy — the grief of losing your grandmother, and with it, that disorienting sense of "what now?" that can make the future feel almost unrecognizable. I can hear in the way you're speaking that this sadness runs really deep, even as you're reaching out, which actually takes a quiet kind of courage. You're right that talking won't bring her back, but it can help us gently untangle some of that weight together, and find a way to hold her memory while still finding meaning in what's ahead.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly, the part about "finding meaning in what's ahead" feels kind of hollow to me right now. Like, my grandmother was the person I called when things got hard, and now that line is just... gone, and I don't know how to fill that silence. I guess I'm skeptical that any amount of talking is going to make that feel less empty.
therapist: That hollowness you're describing makes complete sense — she wasn't just a person in your life, she was a specific kind of anchor, and no reframe or conversation is going to simply replace that. I notice you're pushing back on the idea of "finding meaning," and I want to honor that rather than rush past it, because your skepticism isn't resistance — it's grief being honest. For now, we don't have to fix the silence or fill it; we can just sit with what it actually feels like to have lost that voice.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually helps a little, just hearing that I don't have to fix it right now. Because I think part of what's been making it worse is this pressure I put on myself to like, get back to normal, and when I can't, I feel guilty on top of everything else. It's like I'm grieving her and then also beating myself up for not grieving the "right" way.
therapist: The way you're speaking — there's a kind of urgency there, like even describing this pressure feels pressing and a little overwhelming — and what you're naming is so important: grief layered with self-judgment is an exhausting double burden. That critical voice telling you you're grieving "wrong" is actually a thought we can gently examine together, because there is no right way, and the fact that you're struggling isn't a failure — it's a reflection of how much she meant to you. What does that inner critic usually sound like when it tells you you're not doing this well enough?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It usually sounds something like "you should be functioning better by now, it's been a month" or "other people have dealt with worse and they're fine." And then I start comparing myself to this imaginary person who somehow handles loss gracefully, which just makes me feel even more alone in it. I don't know if examining that voice is really going to quiet it, because it feels so convinced it's right.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, softly, like you're carrying something delicate — matches exactly what you're describing: a voice that feels very certain and very close, and it makes sense that it feels convincing because it's been repeating itself unchallenged for a while. But notice what that critic is actually doing: it's comparing your insides to an imaginary person's outsides, which is never a fair fight. We don't need to silence it all at once — we just need to start asking it for evidence, because "a month should be enough" isn't a fact, it's an assumption, and assumptions can be questioned.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying about asking it for evidence, but in the moment when that voice kicks in, I'm not exactly in a calm, logical headspace where I can just cross-examine it. It's more like it hits me out of nowhere and I'm already feeling terrible before I even realize what's happening. I guess I'm worried that the technique sounds reasonable here but will just fall apart when I'm actually in the middle of it.
therapist: Your concern is completely valid, and honestly it shows real self-awareness — there's a difference between understanding something in a calm moment and being able to use it when the wave hits. The goal isn't to become a cool-headed debater in your worst moments; it's actually to practice noticing the voice *just enough* that you create a tiny sliver of space between it hitting and you fully believing it — and that comes with small, repeated practice, not perfection. So rather than cross-examining it in the storm, we might start with something simpler: just learning to recognize it and name it, like "there's that voice again," which is a much gentler first step than arguing back.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Okay, "there's that voice again" feels a little more manageable than trying to dismantle it on the spot, I'll give you that. But I guess my worry is that even just noticing it might bring me right back to thinking about her and feeling that wave of missing her all over again. It's like I'm not sure I want to poke at it, even gently, because I don't know what's going to come out.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — quickly, with a kind of tightness — tells me that even talking about poking at it feels a little scary, like you're bracing for something. That fear of the wave makes complete sense, and it's actually worth naming: you're not avoiding grief because you're weak, you're avoiding it because you loved her deeply and that pain is real. We can go as slowly as you need — noticing the voice doesn't have to mean diving into the full weight of missing her, and you get to decide how much of the door to open at any given time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually means something to me, the part about deciding how much of the door to open. I think I've been operating like it's all or nothing, like if I start feeling it I have to feel all of it at once, and that's terrifying. Maybe that's part of why I've been keeping myself so busy, because stopping feels like standing at the edge of something I might fall into.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, quickly, with a kind of heightened tension — feels like someone standing very carefully near that edge you just described, and I want you to know that makes complete sense. What you've just identified is really significant: the busyness isn't avoidance for no reason, it's been protecting you from what felt like a free fall, and that's actually a very human and understandable response to something this big. But here's what's worth holding onto — a door you control isn't a cliff edge, and learning to open it just a crack, then close it again, is exactly the kind of practice that can make the grief feel less like something that will swallow you whole.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: The idea of opening it just a crack and then being able to close it again is something I want to believe, but I'm not sure I trust myself to actually close it once it's open. Like, what if I try to feel a little bit of it and it just takes over, and then I'm useless for the rest of the day, and I have work and responsibilities I can't just fall apart over. I guess I'm scared that I don't have that kind of control over my own emotions.
therapist: The pitch and pace in your voice right now tells me this fear feels very real and very present, not abstract — and I want to gently offer a different frame: the fact that you've been holding this grief together while working and functioning for a whole month actually suggests you have more capacity than you're giving yourself credit for. The fear that emotions will "take over" is itself a thought we can examine, because most people find that feelings, when given just a little room, tend to move through rather than take over permanently. And practically speaking, we can actually practice this together in small, structured ways — so the first time you crack the door, you're not doing it alone or without a plan to close it again.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hadn't really thought about it that way, that getting through this month at all is actually evidence of something. But I think part of me is also afraid that if I start to believe I can handle it, and then I can't, that'll just be one more thing to feel bad about. I guess the idea of practicing it here with you feels slightly less terrifying than doing it alone, though I'm still not totally convinced I won't just shut down the moment things get too real.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a kind of high, tight energy — sounds like someone who is genuinely trying to reach toward something hopeful while bracing for disappointment at the same time, and that makes complete sense given what you've been through. What you just named is actually a really important pattern: the fear of trying and failing feels worse than not trying at all, which is a form of self-protection that's kept you safe but also kept you stuck. The fact that you're willing to practice this here, even with that fear present, is itself a small crack in the door — and shutting down if things get too real isn't failure, it's just information we work with together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think what's getting to me right now is that phrase "information we work with together," because it makes it sound like there's some kind of safety net, and part of me really wants to believe that. But I also notice I keep waiting for the catch, like at some point you're going to say something that makes me feel like I'm doing this wrong too. I guess that's probably that same critical voice showing up again, just pointed in a different direction this time.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now feels like someone thinking very fast, almost outpacing themselves — and yet what you just did is actually remarkable: you caught that critical voice in real time, mid-conversation, and named it for exactly what it is. That's not a small thing. And I want to be straightforward with you — there is no catch, and there's no way to do this wrong here, but I also think the fact that you're waiting for one tells us something important about how long that voice has been running in the background, not just about grief, but about whether you're ever quite enough.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
